params.text:
The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974

This Act is the foundation of workplace health and safety in Great Britain and the main piece of health and safety law in England, enforced by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE). It places a duty on your employer to protect the health, safety and welfare of everyone affected by their work — you, the people you support, visitors and members of the public — and it sets out duties for employees too.

Your employer must do this “so far as is reasonably practicable”. In plain terms, they must weigh the size of a risk against the time, trouble and cost of controlling it, and take sensible steps rather than ignore hazards or spend money on dangers that are trivial.

What your employer must do

  • Provide a safe workplace, safe equipment and safe systems of work.
  • Give you the information, instruction, training and supervision you need to work safely.
  • Carry out risk assessments and put sensible controls in place.
  • Provide any personal protective equipment (PPE) free of charge.

What you must do

  • Take reasonable care of your own health and safety and that of anyone affected by what you do (or fail to do).
  • Co-operate with your employer on health and safety — follow procedures and safe systems of work.
  • Use things properly — use equipment and substances the way you were trained to, and never misuse or interfere with anything provided for safety.
  • Report problems — tell your employer about hazards, faults, accidents, near misses and gaps in protection.

The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 build on the Act, make risk assessment an explicit legal requirement, and require your employer to carry out risk assessments and give you information and training.

params.alt: A care worker, beside the heading “The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974”. Key points: Take reasonable care; Co-operate; Use things properly.

params.question: You are asked to use a stand-aid hoist you have never been trained on to move Mr Okafor, who cannot weight-bear. What is the correct action?

answers.text: Decline to use it until you have been trained and follow the person's moving-and-handling plan, explaining why to your senior.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Both the law and your duty of care mean you should not use equipment you are untrained on. Get trained and follow the care plan.

answers.text: Have a go anyway so Mr Okafor isn't kept waiting.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Using unfamiliar equipment risks serious injury to Mr Okafor and to you. You must be trained first.

answers.text: Move him by hand with a colleague instead, lifting under his arms.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Drag-lifting under the arms is unsafe and can cause shoulder injury and skin damage. Use the correct equipment following training and the care plan.

answers.text: Ignore the plan and use a different hoist you prefer.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: You must follow the person's individual moving-and-handling plan and only use equipment you are competent and authorised to use.

params.question: Under health and safety law, which of these is a duty that falls on YOU as an employee rather than on your employer?

answers.text: Taking reasonable care of your own safety and co-operating with safe systems of work.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Act gives employees a duty to take reasonable care and to co-operate with the arrangements their employer puts in place.
Incorrect. Arranging risk assessments is the employer’s duty under the 1999 Regulations, though you help by reporting hazards.

answers.text: Paying for the protective equipment you need.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Your employer must provide necessary protective equipment free of charge; the cost is not yours to carry.

answers.text: Writing the organisation’s health and safety policy.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Producing the policy is an employer responsibility, not something expected of a care worker.
